items.title: St. Catherine Monastery’s land ownership lawsuits adjourned after archbishop backs Egypt-Greece deal
items.description: St. Catherine’s Monastery’s archbishop said on Saturday that he intends to sign an agreement with the Egyptian government that would organize the religious community’s relationship to the monastery and surrounding lands where they have based their spiritual life for over 1,400 years. Egypt’s government had put forward a draft proposal in July that would consolidate ownership of the monastery and surrounding lands in the hands of the Egyptian state for the first time, following decades of dispute over the status of the religious sanctuary in South Sinai, which has effectively been independent of state and legal frameworks, since its history at the site predates these frameworks’ jurisdiction. The dispute had escalated when the Ismailia Court of Appeals issued a 2025 ruling establishing the state’s ownership of the monastery lands, granting the monastery’s usufruct rights to occupy and manage a majority of the property but ordering the expulsion of the monastery’s then-archbishop from a portion of the lands on the grounds that he had seized them unlawfully. The ruling precipitated a series of competing claims to the monastery and its lands and a crisis over the monastery’s leadership. Those competing claims are poised for resolution following the archbishop’s indication over the weekend that he would agree to the government’s proposal, although the former archbishop voiced condemnation for the agreement on Saturday, claiming the religious community is being pressured to accept. With Symeon Papadopoulos, the archbishop of Sinai, Pharan and Raitho, stating that he intends to sign an agreement with the Egyptian government that would bring an end to the pending legal proceedings and disputes over the monastery’s status, a parallel legal process that sought to challenge the court ruling was postponed on Sunday by the Ismailia Court of Appeals. While the 2025 ruling had upheld the government’s ownership of the monastery and surrounding lands, the court was still reviewing the monastery’s ongoing challenge to the ruling in favor of the case’s complainants: the South Sinai Governorate, the antiquities minister and the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency’s head. The court, sitting in the Tor circuit and presided over by judge Alaa Abdel Razeq, nevertheless adjourned the cases until December 27, citing the need for the parties to establish in the case files the legal capacity of the person running the monastery’s affairs. Papadopoulos has said he will arrange a date to sign the agreement with the monks and the Egyptian government “as soon as his health permits.” The archbishop’s announcement was welcomed with relief from both the Egyptian and Greek governments. In a statement published on Saturday, the Foreign Ministry said it had received a letter from Papadopoulos confirming he would sign the contract concerning the monastery and the surrounding lands “once a date for the [signing] ceremony is set.” The statement also said the agreement upholds the Ismailia Court of Appeals ruling “in full compliance with relevant national legislation, bringing all legal proceedings to an end.” Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis, meanwhile, thanked Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and Foreign Minister Badr Abdel Atty for what he described as their role in making the agreement possible. In a statement, Gerapetritis said the agreement “ensures, in perpetuity, the preservation of the Monastery’s religious character and that of its ecclesiastical properties, as well as the continuity of the Monastery through the granting of long-term residence permits to its monks.” The monastery’s lawyer, Fathy Ragheb, however, told Mada Masr that legal proceedings are still pending before the Court of Cassation and the Court of Appeals, with no final rulings so far. Ragheb asked for more time to consult with officials responsible for the monastery before providing further comment on the fate of these cases. Mada Masr also attempted to reach representatives of the monastery for comment but received no response as of time of publication. Former Archbishop Damianos’s position stood in even starker contrast to the welcome from Egyptian and Greek state officials. Damianos accused the Greek government, represented by the prime and foreign ministers, of exerting “unbearable” pressure on the monks in recent days to force them to sign what he described as a “shameful and unacceptable” settlement with the Egyptian state. “I am sure that my brothers will not open the back door for the fall of our Holy Monastery,” he added. Damianos also said that the Greek government circulated information that Egypt’s Court of Cassation could issue a final ruling on Saturday in the monastery’s case, in a bid to pressure Papadopoulos and the monks into signing the agreement proposed by the Egyptian government. Commenting on Papadopoulos’s stated intention to conclude the deal, Damianos said he was “saddened” by the decision, adding that the archbishop’s remarks neither disclosed the terms of the proposed settlement nor indicated that the other monks had consented to it, as required under the monastery’s statutes. He stressed that Papadopoulos has no right to unilaterally sign any settlement that would entail relinquishing “centuries-old historical titles.” Damianos’ 52-year leadership of the monastery came to an abrupt end in 2025. The conclusion of his leadership was precipitated by the Ismailia court ruling, which included orders to evict Damanios, in his capacity as the archbishop of St. Catherine’s Monastery at the time, from 14 disputed properties in the monastery compound in South Sinai on the grounds that he had seized the land without legal basis and carried out construction without official permits. The former archbishop claimed on Saturday that he had established an out-of-court agreement with the Egyptian government, before the 2025 court ruling, that would have seen the government explicitly and unreservedly recognize the Holy Monastery of Sinai as owner of all 71 disputed properties. The agreement was never formally signed, he said, and instead, the Ismailia Court of Appeals emerged on May 28, 2025 to affirm the Egyptian government’s ownership of the monastery’s lands, granting the monastery usufruct rights only to 57 of the total 71 properties. “The agreement was not signed because the Egyptian government, with which Mr. Gerapetritis was supposedly negotiating, allowed the decision of the Ismailia appeal court to be issued,” added Damanios. “The issue is not only legal; it is primarily political,” he continued. “No one can hide behind the decisions of Egyptian ‘justice’ in order to evade their own responsibilities.” Damanios’s response to the court ruling at the time, however, was to endorse a Greek draft law that would have handed sweeping control over the monastery’s assets to an Athens-based public authority. The move prompted a dispute over his leadership, to which he responded by sending a private guard down to throw a number of monks out of the monastery in retaliation, drawing the Patriarchate’s intervention. In a document compiled by the monks detailing their grievances and sent to Mada Masr at the time, they described Damianos’s move to locate the monastery’s assets under a legal framework in Greece without consulting them and obtaining the approval mandated by the monastery’s statutes as “the ultimate betrayal of the monastery” and a culmination of a longer breakdown in trust. The monastery’s monks voted to depose Damianos and unanimously elected Papadopoulos in his place, though there were no other nominees. An informed source told Mada Masr at the time that figures in the Greek Orthodox Church had refused to grant rival candidates ecclesiastical release to put their names forward. In July, the Egyptian government, represented by its foreign and justice ministers, presented Papadopoulos with a new agreement containing several provisions. Chief among them was recognition of the monastery as an Egyptian legal religious entity, granting the monks “religious possession” of the monastery and its religious institutions — meaning the right to reside on the grounds and practice religious rites — and allowing them to lease the surrounding gardens and land from the Egyptian government for a nominal fee over an extended period, a source close to the monastery told Mada Masr at the time on condition of anonymity. Its abbot and monks, who hold Greek, American and Lebanese nationalities, would also be granted three-year, renewable residence permits, according to the source. The foreign and justice ministers had met with Papadopoulos for more than seven hours in July, pushing him to agree to the deal in exchange for a presidential decree ratifying his election and appointment as the monastery’s head, the source said. Papadopoulos had been in a compromised position since his election in 2025, with no official recognition of his post issued by the Egyptian state, according to the source. This has left the archbishop unable to deal with the monastery’s Egyptian bank accounts or conduct transactions with state institutions in South Sinai. The source noted that while Papadopoulos holds a Greek diplomatic passport, which allows him to travel to and from Egypt for two years, the rest of the monks hold 12-month tourist visas that take three months to renew, leaving them with, in reality, only nine months of residency. The proposed arrangement would follow the precedent set by former President Anwar al-Sadat, who had appointed Damianos as archbishop and later granted him Egyptian citizenship. The Egyptian government’s proposed agreement builds off the May 2025 Ismailia court ruling , which recognized the state’s ownership of St. Catherine’s Monastery and its lands while granting the monks limited usufruct rights for religious use and possession. The ruling also placed all dealings involving the properties under the direct supervision of state authorities. The court also ruled that the monastery’s spiritual affiliation with the Greek Orthodox Church does not confer any legal privileges on it within Egypt. The Ismailia court split the disputed lands into four categories. The first covers the land on which the monastery itself is built, along with other plots that hold some churches and shrines. The monks and archbishop were granted what the court termed “religious possession” of these properties for residence and worship, while ownership remains with the state under the supervision of the Supreme Council of Antiquities. The second category comprises lands outside the monastery’s boundaries, which the court incorporated into the St. Catherine Protectorate under the supervision of the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency. The third consists of agricultural land that the court termed “expulsion lands,” ordering the monks be expelled from it on the grounds that they are occupying it by force. The fourth includes several plots with small churches and monastic facilities covered by preliminary contracts between the monastery and the local administrative unit of St. Catherine. The court ruled that these contracts did not transfer ownership but instead established reciprocal obligations. The source close to the monastery, as well as a second one, previously told Mada Masr Greece supports the Egyptian proposal, and Egyptian officials were working to pressure Papadopoulos and the rest of the monks to agree to the terms, despite what the sources said is a relinquishment of the monastery’s land ownership. They also said Egyptian government representatives put forward the new agreement in July after reaching an understanding with the Greek government. The Friends of St. Catherine’s Monastery Facebook page, which reflects the views of a number of monks, described at the time the agreement as a disastrous formula that dismantles the monastery of its rights and deprives it of its ownership. The group argued that the Egyptian and Greek governments were placing their political and economic interests above the spiritual and historical significance of one of the world’s oldest inhabited monasteries where religious rites are still held. The monastery is being sold in the market of political and economic interests in exchange for the energy agreement that Athens seeks to conclude with Cairo, the group stated. The 2025 court ruling established the state’s ownership of the area for the first time, leaving it at the mercy of the state, which can revoke its legal standing at any time, according to Stephan Dömpke, the head of World Heritage Watch, an independent organization dedicated to protecting UNESCO sites, who spoke to Mada Masr at the time of the court ruling. “Being at the mercy of the Egyptian government is what terrifies the monastery and the whole Orthodox Church,” Dömpke told Mada Masr, “especially when considering the tourism developments unfolding around them without their consent.” In 2021, the Egyptian government launched the “Great Transfiguration” project , aimed at transforming the city of St. Catherine into an international center for Abrahamite religions. Since then, large-scale construction has taken place in the city and around the monastery as part of what the government has described as a “developmental and touristic” initiative. The post St. Catherine Monastery’s land ownership lawsuits adjourned after archbishop backs Egypt-Greece deal first appeared on Mada Masr .

items.title: « Escroc », la nouvelle perfusion musicale de Grand Docteur
items.description: Le reggaeman burkinabè Grand Docteur a accordé une interview à Faso7 le 22 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou pour défendre son nouveau clip intitulé « Escroc ». Dans ce titre chanté en mooré, l'artiste dit s'attaquer à la prolifération de personnes qui « apparaissent » et se présentent comme des guérisseurs, des fetichistes, des pasteurs ou des hadja dotés de pouvoirs divins et dont il doute de la probité de certains. Grand Docteur dit d’emblée que son ancêtre Naaba Baongho était féticheur, son grand-père Naaba Na Waam Taõré était féticheur, son père Kouma aussi. Il se revendique lui-même « traditionnaliste pur » . C'est précisément ce bagage qui lui donne, selon lui, la légitimité pour dénoncer. « Je connais ce que ça veut dire, soigner quelqu'un, aider quelqu'un dans la tradition. Et tous ceux qui viennent en disant que Dieu leur a donné le savoir pour soulager la population. Ils n'ont pas payé. C'est ce qu'ils disent. Mais si à un moment donné, ce que Dieu t'a donné gratuitement, pour te voir maintenant, il y a du privé alors que tu ne l'as pas vu en privé pour prendre… Il y a quelque chose qui cloche quelque part » , a-t-il expliqué. Le titre ne vise pas la tradition ni les religions dans leur ensemble, dit-il. Grand Docteur l'a précisé lui-même, en soulignant qu'il s'attaque aux mauvaises graines, pas à ceux qui ont fait leur preuves. « Même chez nous les artistes, il y a des faux artistes. (…). Voilà pourquoi j'interpelle toute la population à la vigilance et à la méfiance » , a-t-il indiqué. Il illustre son propos par le témoignage d'une proche dont la mère malade a refusé les soins médicaux après avoir entendu des témoignages à la radio sur une guérisseuse. La fille a contracté un crédit pour financer cette alternative. La mère marche aujourd'hui avec des béquilles. « Mon rôle, c'est de diagnostiquer, de conscientiser, de prévenir. Depuis des années, je suis dans ça. Chaque mal qui vient, je diagnostique et puis je passe un morceau » , a-t-il dit. De Petit à Grand Docteur : une histoire de survie En marge du sujet principal, Grand Docteur a raconté l'origine de son nom, devenu Grand Docteur après des années passées sous l'appellation Petit Docteur. L'histoire remonte à 1993, quand il arrive à Ouagadougou, travaille comme employé de maison, fabrique des briques en banco, puis pousse une barrique à eau pendant trois ans. Un malaise dans la cour d'un client l'envoie à l'hôpital Yalgado. Il en ressort avec 1 200 francs CFA, toutes ses économies de trois ans dilapidées en ordonnances. Il achète des médicaments de la rue au marché et se lance dans leur revente. Un vendeur plus grand que lui dormait avec lui sur le même trottoir. Pour les distinguer, l'un devient Grand Docteur, l'autre Petit Docteur. Le surnom traverse la photographie, la vente de cassettes, la réparation de téléphones portables, jusqu'à la musique. Le changement de nom est venu d'une leçon reçue en Côte d'Ivoire lors d'un concours où il représentait le Burkina Faso. Des anciens de la musique africaine l'avaient pris à part pour lui citer des artistes dont le nom contenait le mot « Petit » : tous disparus malgré leur talent. « Tu ne peux pas dépasser ton nom. Les conditions vont te faire rester petit » , lui avaient-ils dit. Il a annoncé le changement sur sa page. Pas sans craindre les réactions. « Je connais l'esprit burkinabè. Ils ne vont jamais venir te demander pourquoi ton nom est Grand Docteur. Ils vont juste dire que tu te gonfles. Mais j'étais obligé » , a-t-il confié. Sa carrière, dit-il, se porte bien. Il vit de la musique, il joue dans des villes où il ne pouvait pas aller il y a encore quelques années, grâce aux succès des opérations de reconquête du territoire national. Grand Docteur prépare déjà son prochain titre, qu'il intitulera « Incompris » . Un autoportrait, sans doute. Josué TIENDREBEOGO Faso7 L’article « Escroc », la nouvelle perfusion musicale de Grand Docteur est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: 24 morts dans une collision entre un bus et un camion
items.description: Au moins 24 personnes ont péri et une vingtaine d’autres ont été blessées dans une collision entre un bus et un camion survenue, le dimanche 25 octobre 2026, sur l’autoroute reliant Nairobi à Mombasa, selon la police kényane. Ce drame relance l’alerte sur l’insécurité routière au Kenya, où plus de 5 000 personnes meurent chaque année sur les routes, selon les chiffres avancés par l’Autorité nationale de sécurité des transports. Le Kenya est une nouvelle fois frappé par un drame routier meurtrier. Dimanche 25 octobre 2026, au moins 24 personnes ont perdu la vie dans une violente collision entre un bus et un camion sur l’axe Nairobi-Mombasa, l’une des principales voies de circulation du pays. Le bilan fait, également, état d'une vingtaine de blessés. Plusieurs victimes ont été prises en charge à l’hôpital de Mtito Andei, a indiqué son directeur médical, Paul Kisienya, cité par des médias. Selon les informations rapportées, les passagers du bus rentraient à Mombasa après avoir assisté aux funérailles de leur pasteur dans l’ouest du pays. Les circonstances exactes de la collision restent à déterminer. Un axe routier endeuillé à répétition Ce nouvel accident ravive les inquiétudes autour de la sécurité sur l’autoroute Nairobi-Mombasa. En l’espace de trois semaines, cet axe a été le théâtre de deux accidents meurtriers, le précédent ayant fait 17 morts. Face à cette succession de tragédies, l’Autorité nationale de sécurité des transports réclame que ces accidents soient déclarés catastrophe nationale. L’organisme alerte sur l’ampleur du phénomène, avec environ 20 000 accidents et plus de 5 000 morts recensés chaque année au Kenya. Ruto ordonne l’inspection des véhicules de transport public Au lendemain de ce nouveau drame, le président kényan William Ruto a présenté ses condoléances aux familles endeuillées et ordonné l’inspection de tous les véhicules de transport public. Il a également exhorté les conducteurs à respecter le code de la route. La répétition de ces accidents pose une nouvelle fois la question de l’efficacité des mesures de prévention et du renforcement des contrôles sur les routes du pays. Au-delà du lourd bilan humain de cette collision, l’urgence demeure: éviter que les routes kényanes ne continuent de se transformer en pièges mortels pour leurs usagers. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article 24 morts dans une collision entre un bus et un camion est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: 2e édition de la SNLCC : une journée portes ouvertes à la BCLCC pour sensibiliser sur la cybercriminalité
items.description: Dans le cadre de la 2e édition de la Semaine nationale de lutte contre la cybercriminalité (SNLCC), la Brigade centrale de lutte contre la cybercriminalité (BCLCC) a organisé une journée portes ouvertes (JPO), ce 26 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou. Il s'agit de rapprocher l'institution du grand public afin de le sensibiliser et de prévenir certaines infractions. Cette année, la Semaine nationale de lutte contre la cybercriminalité (SNLCC) se tient sous le thème : « Cybercriminalité et menaces numériques émergentes : du clic au crime ». Elle traduit la nécessité de sensibiliser les populations aux infractions commises sur les réseaux sociaux. Selon le Commandant Ahmed Ouédraogo, secrétaire général du ministère de la Sécurité, cette thématique a été retenue, car la majorité des utilisateurs des plateformes numériques ignorent les réglementations en vigueur, d'où la survenue de certains écarts de comportement. Il a cependant invité les populations à se rendre dans les locaux de la BCLCC afin de s'imprégner des différentes mesures. Les acteurs de la JPO de la BCLCC©️Faso7 « C'est une opportunité qui est offerte à la population de pouvoir se rapprocher des différents acteurs pour mieux être informé, c'est-à-dire avoir toutes les informations nécessaires sur comment utiliser les réseaux sociaux et éviter, en tout cas, de se faire prendre, on va dire, par des écarts de comportement», a-t-il indiqué. Le commissaire principal de Police Akim Nignan, commandant de la BCLCC, a ajouté que cette semaine sera marquée par des sensibilisations à travers une caravane, des panels et un maracana des acteurs. Également, il sera organisé un hackathon au profit des jeunes afin de leur permettre de mettre leur savoir-faire au service de la lutte contre la cybercriminalité. Le commandant de la BCLCC a rappelé que l'objectif est de sensibiliser et de prévenir des cas d'infractions qui ont été commis auparavant. Il est aussi question de fédérer les actions des différents acteurs pour venir à bout de la cybercriminalité. « Nous savions bien que nos populations écoutent et pour cela, nous savions que la sensibilisation qui sera faite va porter donc fruits et nous aurons moins affaire à des populations qui posent des actes malveillants sur les réseaux sociaux » , a expliqué le commissaire principal de Police Akim Nignan. Les JPO de la BCLCC ont réuni différents acteurs, dont l'ARCOD, la Brigade Laabal et l'Office national d'identification. La 2e édition de la SNLCC se déroule du 26 au 30 octobre 2026. Cheick Habib Désiré BAYILI Faso7 L’article 2e édition de la SNLCC : une journée portes ouvertes à la BCLCC pour sensibiliser sur la cybercriminalité est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Filière avicole : Le Burkina Faso lance la formation de 1 000 acteurs
items.description: Le gouvernement burkinabè a lancé, le 24 octobre 2026, à l’École nationale de formation agricole de Matourkou (ENAFA), une campagne de formation de 1 000 acteurs de la filière avicole, dont 763 bassecouriers et 237 gestionnaires de fermes. Inscrite dans le cadre de l’Offensive agropastorale, hydraulique et halieutique 2026-2028, cette initiative vise à renforcer les capacités des acteurs pour accroître la production nationale de poulets de chair, de poussins et d’œufs à couver. À travers ce programme, les autorités ambitionnent de contribuer à la souveraineté alimentaire du Burkina Faso, notamment en réduisant la dépendance du pays aux importations de produits avicoles. Cette vision, portée par le Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, repose entre autres sur le renforcement des compétences techniques et managériales des acteurs de première ligne du secteur de l’élevage. Le Dr Amadou Dicko, ministre délégué chargé des Ressources animales, représentant le ministre d’État, le Commandant Ismaël Sombié, ministre de l’Agriculture, a mis l’accent sur la nécessité de doter les producteurs et les gestionnaires de fermes des connaissances nécessaires pour améliorer durablement les performances de la filière. Le gouvernement a ainsi initié « ce programme ambitieux » afin de renforcer les capacités de 1 000 bénéficiaires issus de différentes localités du pays. Prévue sur une durée de 30 jours, la formation accorde une place importante aux exercices pratiques. Selon le Dr Amadou Dicko, ce calendrier permettra aux apprenants de suivre les différentes étapes de l’élevage d’une bande de volailles, de la réception des poussins jusqu’à l’abattage. L’organisation du programme tient également compte des contraintes et des occupations des participants. Au-delà des apprentissages techniques liés à la conduite des élevages, le programme comprend des modules consacrés au civisme, au patriotisme et aux valeurs morales. Cette approche vise à associer le renforcement des compétences professionnelles à la promotion de valeurs jugées essentielles à l’engagement des acteurs dans le développement national. Renforcer son potentiel de production avicole S’adressant aux 763 bassecouriers et aux 237 gestionnaires de fermes, le ministre délégué a insisté sur les responsabilités spécifiques de chaque catégorie dans le développement de la filière. Pour les bassecouriers, l’accent sera mis sur la maîtrise des techniques de biosécurité, l’alimentation des volailles et le suivi sanitaire. Ces compétences sont essentielles pour limiter les risques de maladies, réduire les pertes et améliorer les conditions d’élevage. Les gestionnaires de fermes, quant à eux, seront outillés pour renforcer leurs capacités en matière de gestion technique, financière et logistique. La maîtrise de ces différents aspects constitue un levier important pour améliorer la rentabilité des exploitations et assurer leur viabilité économique. À travers cette formation différenciée, le gouvernement entend agir à la fois sur les pratiques d’élevage et sur la gestion des unités de production. L’objectif est de disposer d’acteurs mieux préparés à répondre à la demande nationale en produits avicoles. Selon Émilien Bakoné, directeur général de la production animale, les participants proviennent de divers horizons du Burkina Faso. Leur sélection a été effectuée sur la base de critères objectifs définis par un comité national. Au total, 2 000 candidatures ont été enregistrées pour cette campagne, témoignant de l’intérêt suscité par cette initiative auprès des acteurs de la filière. Avec la formation de ces 1 000 bénéficiaires, le Burkina Faso entend renforcer son potentiel de production avicole. Cette action s’inscrit dans une stratégie plus large visant à couvrir les besoins nationaux en poulets de chair, en poussins et en œufs à couver, tout en consolidant les bases d’une filière avicole plus performante et moins dépendante de l’extérieur. items.title: A Map for Loving America
items.description: S tevie Wonder’s outfit seemed, at first, to be a strange choice. It was September 1976, and the 26-year-old Grammy winner, better known at that point for appearing on his album covers with a short afro or in cornrows and a tunic, was wearing a cowboy outfit: a collared, cream-colored shirt and matching trousers, a terra-cotta bandanna around his neck, a wide-brimmed hat. He also had a double holster wrapped around his hips, reading: NUMBER ONE WITH A BULLET . Maureen Orth, then a young writer for Newsweek , was confused. Along with a herd of other journalists, she had traveled to a 145-acre farm in North Brookfield, Massachusetts, for a listening party for Songs in the Key of Life —Wonder’s new, 17-track album, which he was releasing along with a four-track EP, for a grand total of 105 minutes of soul-stirring sound. Western iconography hadn’t been on the menu, or so she thought. “It’s like, what? Stevie, you’re a cowboy? Why?” Orth recalled on the 2024 podcast The Wonder of Stevie , which I co-created and co-produced. (Wonder executive-produced.) “We haven’t heard the songs yet, but there aren’t any cowboy songs on the record.” Orth was right: Nothing on the album sounded remotely like a cowboy song. But Wonder’s getup wasn’t so much about communicating the content of his opus as it was about playfully claiming the context around it. And that context was that he, a uniquely brilliant symbol of American promise, had sought and captured something uniquely, brilliantly American. Five decades later, Songs ’ message—one of optimism, resolve, and self-belief in the shadow of hyper-partisan politics and communities coming apart—still feels urgent. Which makes it seem right that Wonder recently began a 17-city tour across Europe and the United States to mark the 50th anniversary of the record’s release, putting on shows in which he is playing the entire album. A lot was going on in the country back when Songs came out. It was the United States’ bicentennial, and although the nation had reason to celebrate, people also had much to mourn: race riots, economic recession, repeated paroxysms from the corrupt presidency of Richard Nixon. At the time, Wonder had been experiencing a sadness and disillusionment about politics and U.S. foreign policy so profound that he had seriously considered leaving the music business and moving to Ghana, where he planned to work with disabled children. “You can sing about things and talk about things,” he had said earlier in the ’70s, “but if your actions don’t speak louder than your words, you’re nothing.” Wonder had gone so far as to announce a “farewell” tour. (Some believed this was a tactic to get a better deal as he renegotiated his contract with his label, Tamla, a division of Motown Records.) When Songs arrived, then, it seemed to be a reassertion of his primacy within American popular culture—and perhaps of his belief in America itself. Time magazine reported that the album took Wonder more than two years to produce. It cooked for so long that Motown executives had T-shirts made featuring a play on the phrase that Wonder kept using when asked about the project’s status: WE’RE ALMOST FINISHED . What they didn’t know was that Wonder, rather than struggling, was perfecting the simple message at the album’s heart—that to express love for America requires not only celebrating it with fireworks and flags but also acknowledging its missteps and failings. S ongs is a deeply personal album for millions of people. (The singer-songwriter India.Arie, born in 1975, has described it as a record that “feels like family.”) In fact, I’d initially thought of starting this article by describing how the record was the primary soundtrack to my early life—from the weekend afternoons of my childhood, when I studied the album’s liner notes and lyrics as my dad’s turntable crackled in the background, to one particularly tumultuous year during my 20s, when, rocked by a breakup, I shut myself in my bedroom, slid a disc into my CD player, and sang along to “I Wish,” “Joy Inside My Tears,” and “As.” Over the years, I came to realize that the album owes much of its enduring power to its relevance as a source of personal and political optimism. It is a love letter to the listener but also a message, marked urgent , to a nation. When I say that Songs in the Key of Life —consistently voted one of the best albums of all time—is uniquely American, I mean that it is both by America and of it. At that farm in 1976, Wonder’s outfit was a clever play on his argument about his country, but his songs provided the substance. They spoke of love and hope and faith and history and family and even fear. The first track, “Love’s in Need of Love Today,” offered a quiet opener with a devastating message: The country was veering from its imagined ideal. Hate was “goin’ ’round,” Wonder sang, “Breaking many hearts / Stop it please / Before it’s gone too far.” The album’s third song, “Village Ghetto Land,” was where things started to get real. It was a nearly three-and-a-half-minute indictment of the economic and geographical segregation visited on America’s less fortunate, set to sober, almost mournful electronic strings. From there, the record unfolded like a map of the United States’ psyche, the soundtrack of a people (well, some people) who were wrestling with the gap between the stated promise of this country and its sobering reality. Its eighth song, “Pastime Paradise”—which later inspired the 1995 Coolio hit “Gangsta’s Paradise”—was about coming to terms with an idealized past that had never actually existed. The lyrics chide people who glorify times “long gone behind,” those “wasting most their days / In remembrance of ignorance oldest praise.” Wonder cautions those living with a romanticized view of history against succumbing to inertia. He invites those whose nostalgia blinds them to the present to confront the truth of the past, to move toward a brighter future. “Tell me, who of them will come to be?” he sang. “How many of them are you and me?” Then there was “Black Man,” perhaps the album’s most explicitly political track: a head-thumping, funk-inflected assertion about people of color’s contributions to the creation of America. Name-dropping figures including Squanto and Sacagawea, Benjamin Banneker and Harriet Tubman, Wonder sang: We pledge allegiance All our lives To the magic colors Red, blue, and white But we all must be given The liberty that we defend For with justice not for all men History will repeat again It’s time we learned This world was made for all men F or years, rumors circulated that Wonder had considered dozens or even more than 100 songs for inclusion on the record, many of which people never would have heard. So it was a delight when, on the date of the album’s anniversary this year, September 28, he surprised the music world by releasing on streaming services Songs in the Key of Life—The EP , a quartet of previously unreleased tracks from the era when he was recording the original album. I was excited at first. But after listening to the EP a few times, I felt uninspired. I wanted more than what I’d heard (lyrics mostly about love, loss, and regret). So, I reached out to the cultural critic Wesley Morris, a Stevie stan like I am, and the host of The Wonder of Stevie. I wrote to him that one of the “new” songs (“It’s Easier”) felt a little stale, reminiscent of Wonder’s 1971 work Where I’m Coming From . “I’m Into Livin’” felt very Hotter Than July , the album that Wonder released four years after Songs in the Key of Life . And the others seemed like sentimental-bordering-on-empty attempts at saying something that—well, I couldn’t quite figure it out. To be clear, I was in a horrible mood. The promise of America that Wonder had celebrated in Songs has been feeling, to me, further away than ever. The Trump administration has been unraveling many of the rights that previous generations worked so hard and long to ensure. It has been unleashing violent law enforcement in cities across the country; instigating political witch hunts ; trying to make it harder to vote ; and, contra “Black Man,” attempting to control how our national history is told, in part by downplaying the role that women and people of color have played in the political and cultural project that is America. I was also frustrated. All this strife, all the ways in which the world has gone backwards, and Wonder had released four new songs about love? Then I remembered something that Morris had said on The Wonder of Stevie : “Anytime you hear a Black American singing about love, what you’re hearing is a choice not to be singing about a dozen other things. Being poor, getting ripped off, going to court or prison, driving your brother or your cousin to court, visiting them in prison. Talking about how affirmative action doesn’t need to end. Talking about voting rights and why that’s important.” When these are the realities people are facing, a song about love—romance, love of people, love of community—can become its own declaration of independence. “In its own quiet way,” Morris said on the podcast, “a Black love song says, Here. Here’s my heart . And despite all of this other shit—betrayal, neglect, struggle, rage, lunacy, the pernicious old status quo,” he added, Wonder is asking: “ Would you look at the world? How is it that I can know all of this and still make this gorgeous, contiguously gorgeous sound that is this whole album? This is the story of us all .” That story evolves in fits and starts, and circles back on itself before moving forward—in a pattern somewhat similar to the cover art for Songs in the Key of Life , which to me evokes a spiral of warm, heavenly clouds. Wonder, a modern griot, understands that people need to tell stories to make sense of a complicated world, and that they need to believe in those stories to keep faith. As he sings in “Sir Duke,” the album’s fifth song and an homage to great American songwriters and singers such as Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Louis Armstrong, and Ella Fitzgerald, “Music is a world within itself.” With Songs , Wonder created a soundtrack, too, a picture of the world as it was—and of what it could become.

items.title: The Collapse of Cuba
items.description: Photographs by Moises Saman This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. A priest led me up battered stairs to a tiny room at the top of a church. From the window, we gazed down at the decayed colonial villas and scattered trash fires of eastern Havana. He pointed to the yellow wall behind us, where someone had sketched a meticulous map of the local street grid. “They posted armed guards here, to watch over us,” he said. Cuba’s Communist government, the priest said, took over the convent, cloister, and school of Los Escolapios after the revolution of 1959, expelling the nuns and setting up a guard post—one part of the regime’s sprawling apparatus of surveillance and control. The church downstairs was virtually closed, the congregation mostly exiled or jailed in accordance with Communist Cuba’s atheist principles. The guards are gone now, along with the portraits of Fidel Castro and the secular schoolteachers who commandeered the convent’s lower floors after the revolution. The church is in the process of reclaiming the magnificent 18th-century cloister from the state, which left it in ruins. The priest, Iván Guerra Álvarez, made clear he believes that history is approaching another turning point, and that the Communist regime will soon be gone. “The Church will play a big role in the transition,” he told me. “We are the biggest institution in Cuba outside the government.” No one can say when or how that transition will happen. Donald Trump may or may not have “the honor of taking Cuba,” as he boasted after imposing an oil blockade on the island earlier this year. The Cuban regime has stifled any viable domestic opposition. But the withering of the state—a process that has been under way for decades—has accelerated, and is shocking to see up close. The ration cards that used to guarantee basic foodstuffs for every Cuban had been blank for weeks when I visited in August. Police and soldiers were once ubiquitous throughout the country, but I saw hardly any. In far-eastern Cuba, I met a fisherman who told me that he and others like him, who lacked electricity for refrigeration, have gone back to traditional methods of drying and salting fish. The average monthly salary for public-sector employees in Cuba—including doctors and teachers—is about 6,500 pesos, which is less than $10 and far below the cost of a subsistence diet (a single carton of eggs can cost up to 4,700 pesos). Even getting small amounts of cash can be a trial: Banks sometimes limit withdrawals to 1,000 pesos (less than $1.50) per person per day. Moises Saman / Magnum for The Atlantic A former boarding school in Cienfuegos, established after the 1959 Revolution, where students combined classroom education with agricultural labor The government still purports—on faded billboards, in party speeches—to meet all of the material and spiritual needs of its citizens, but it is now bankrupt in every sense . Almost no one believes in the system anymore, and many, especially outside Havana, behave as if the government simply does not exist. As in the Soviet-dominated Eastern bloc during its final years, destitution is leading people back to older faiths. Afro Cuban Santeria and Catholicism have flourished, and “house churches” have proliferated, often evangelical and sometimes consisting of nothing more than a dozen folding chairs in someone’s living room. Guerra Álvarez led me down from the church tower to the main sanctuary of Los Escolapios, an atmospheric shift he half-jokingly likened to a trip from North to South Korea. We found ourselves in a noisy crowd of more than 100 schoolchildren and worshippers. A teacher dressed as an angel, with a white beard, wig, and gown, was giving Bible lessons in the dimly lit nave. Afterward, volunteers handed out lunches of rice and beans. To see so many people looking so cheerful was striking; Cuba is now a country full of empty streets and abandoned buildings, having lost as much as a quarter of its population to migration in the past few years. The expanded role of the churches is partly an outcome of American policy: The U.S. government has long favored the Catholic Church as an intermediary. When the Trump administration approved a $100 million aid package for Cuba in May, it was on the condition that the funds be distributed by faith-based groups and humanitarian organizations. But the rise of religion in Cuba is also a measure of the state’s withdrawal—and perhaps a hint at the island’s future direction. Moises Saman / Magnum for The Atlantic Teens receive bread and drinks at a Catholic church in Havana. I came to Cuba expecting to see suffering. What I did not anticipate was the near-total collapse of the state. This was evident even in Havana, where all-day blackouts are routine, but things are much worse in the eastern half of the island, which has long been poorer and less developed. Cuba’s religious revival has burned brightest there, especially among Pentecostal churches, whose traditions include faith healing and miracles. [ The David Frum show: Cuba is collapsing. Will Trump invade? ] I drove to the east with the photographer Moises Saman, an 18-hour journey that sometimes made us feel as if we were traveling back in time. Weaving slowly among enormous potholes, we passed few other cars. As we got closer to Santiago de Cuba, Cuba’s second-largest city, we saw almost as many horse-drawn carts as motorized vehicles. Moises Saman / Magnum for The Atlantic A weathered roadside billboard, bearing a portrait of Fidel Castro, reads, “ Son las ideas las que nos hacen un pueblo combatiente ” (“It is ideas that make us a fighting people). Poverty is not new in the country, but the number of street beggars I saw shocked me. On the seafront in Santiago, a mother and daughter approached me, both of them skeletally thin, to ask for money. The mother, a white-haired 76-year-old, told me that their only means of support had been her son, who had worked as a security guard and died of cancer last year. Now they spend all day begging and collecting plastic bottles in the hopes of trading them for a few pesos, she said. They get nothing from the state. Later, I visited their home, a filthy ground-floor room where they sleep on metal bed frames topped with cardboard instead of mattresses. When I asked whether there was any electricity, the mother said that they did not even have a bulb. Moises Saman / Magnum for The Atlantic The collapse of the state has left impoverished Cubans with few options besides begging or relying on charity. The failure of Cuba’s health-care system may be the most damning indictment of its Communist regime. Castro once held up the country’s network of local clinics as a model for the world, visible proof that socialism could triumph where capitalism had failed. He sent hundreds of thousands of doctors overseas, an “army of white coats” to bolster Cuba’s image and generate money for the state. (It later emerged that the doctors had been given little choice and many were victims of what has been called forced labor.) Some doctors are still being sent abroad, but more have simply fled Cuba. On Cayo Granma, an island at the entrance to the bay of Santiago, I found a single nurse caring not only for all 870 residents but also for many people from the neighboring coastal areas. She no longer knows how many people she is responsible for, because doctors have been leaving the region so fast that she cannot keep track of the patients forced to seek new care. Her name is Clara Luaces, a woman of 55 with a direct gaze and an air of brisk competence. Her clinic was a room the size of a large closet, hot and crowded with patients when I arrived; outside, it was almost 100 degrees. A 12-year-old boy with a fever sat on a bench, an IV drip in his arm; a girl with a skin infection sat nearby with her mother. “We have to work miracles here,” Luaces said, answering my questions as she checked the boy’s pulse and adjusted his IV. The government had stopped piping water to the island three months earlier, she said, and the resulting lack of clean water had led to a sharp rise in bacterial fevers and skin infections. “Even young people are dying on me,” she said. She was chronically short on medicine and had very little money of her own to supplement the clinic’s supply. The boy began moaning, and Luaces comforted him, putting a pillow under his head and calling him “sweetheart.” “I’m not going to retire,” she said, looking up at me, “because there is no one else to take this on.” Luaces did not want to talk about politics. She confined herself to saying that she had been a student during what Castro dubbed the “special period” in the 1990s, when Cuba went through a severe economic crisis after losing its Soviet patron and the regime seemed on the brink of collapse. What is happening now, she said, is “much more special.” Moises Saman / Magnum for The Atlantic Two people sit outside a house during a nighttime power outage in Camagüey. Others lashed out directly at the state. Not long ago, the country bristled with informants working for the Committees for the Defense of the Revolution. But when I asked people about the CDR, some laughed, and few seemed worried about being overheard. One evening on a beach in Baracoa, a man in his 30s asked me what I thought about Communism. He was lying in a hammock talking with four other men, drinking cheap sugarcane rum from a plastic bottle; they had been complaining about the ever higher prices of rice, beans, and other basic foods. I told him I thought Communism was a lousy way to run a country. He looked squarely at me and said, “I shit on Fidel Castro’s mother.” The other men laughed. He uttered a few more obscenities. Then, suddenly, all of the humor drained from the man’s face. His voice went taut with anger, and tears welled up in his eyes. “Cuba is frozen in time!” he shouted. “There’s no hope. It’s a sad thing to be born a Cuban. That’s what I think, and I don’t care; they can send me to prison if they want.” The other men had gone silent. Here is another measure of Cubans’ anger at their government: During nine days of travel around the island, I did not meet a single person who blamed Donald Trump or the United States for their situation. I sometimes reminded them about the blockade Trump had started earlier this year , cutting Cubans off from the cheap oil that Venezuela had been supplying before the U.S. military captured Nicolás Maduro in January. Hadn’t things gotten worse since then? [ Read: Cuba’s old economic model is ‘exhausted’ ] “I don’t see any change since January,” a retired engineer named Guillermo Almeida told me. “That oil from Venezuela wasn’t reaching the people anyway.” He and others said that the more important turning point was the coronavirus pandemic, which destroyed Cuba’s tourism industry and shrank the value of remittances from family members abroad that many Cubans depend on, exposing more fully a state that had long been depleted. Another man put it differently: “It seems to us that the real embargo is inside of Cuba.” The churches have taken on much of the Cuban state’s old role in keeping people alive. In Baracoa, I met Raul de Jesus Muñoz Munder, a Pentecostal pastor who has been evangelizing in the area for 32 years. He had seen hunger and deprivation, he said, including during the years he spent in a tiny church in the mountains, but nothing as bad as the present. Muñoz Munder described his work almost as if it were a military operation. Every week, he said, he meets with a team of associate pastors at his church, and each man reports on the situation in his home neighborhood: who is sick and needs medicine, who needs food, and how to get it to them. The pastor’s congregation has about 1,100 regular members, but he provides aid to a much larger group. His denomination, the Assemblies of God, has expanded from two to 40 churches in the Baracoa region over the past three decades. The growth of the evangelical movement is hard to quantify in Cuba, where the Catholic Church was once almost universal. No independent numbers on religious affiliation exist—the government has long had a lock on surveys. But everyone I spoke with, both inside and outside the country, agreed that the evangelical presence has surged in recent years. Moises Saman / Magnum for The Atlantic The pastor and a church secretary at the Iglesia Evangélica Pentecostal Asambleas de Dios de Baracoa, in Baracoa, in eastern Cuba. The congregation is one of the city’s most active Protestant churches. In Baracoa, I stumbled upon several different evangelical services one Saturday evening, each of them loud and raucous, the congregation on its feet and clapping along. These kinds of scenes are still a little jarring to many older Cubans. They tend to associate church with more orderly Catholic rituals, and grew up without seeing much of the flamboyant evangelical religiosity that has become common across Latin America. But the island is changing. I heard a fair amount of God talk even on the street. One afternoon in Camagüey, a beautiful, decaying city in east-central Cuba, an elderly woman in a wheelchair called out to me as I passed her open front door. “We have to tell people that God exists,” she said, in an urgent tone. “God’s word has to be fulfilled in its entirety.” One of her children had left the country, and the other one, a high-school teacher, was in prison; she said he’d been given a 14-year sentence for accusing a high-ranking official of corruption. The old woman was living alone, and the only thing she had left was her faith. In Havana, I visited a nursing home owned by the Catholic Church that was full of former civil servants and military officers. In one room I found a dozen old men, their beds lined up about a yard apart. Each had a single narrow locker for all of his earthly possessions. A nurse gave me permission to speak with residents but cautioned me that they were “very sad.” Many of them, she explained, had had distinguished government careers but had found themselves abandoned by both the state and their family at the end of their life. In many cases, their children had left the country. Moises Saman / Magnum for The Atlantic People in need receive a meal at the Concatedral de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción, a Catholic cathedral in Baracoa. One of the men, a wiry 65-year-old, had fought for two years in Angola, where Castro had sent hundreds of thousands of soldiers in the 1970s and ’80s to support a Communist-aligned government. The former soldier had once been a fan of the revolution; you could tell because he had a big tattoo of Che Guevara on his right arm. He’d gotten it when he was 18. He showed me several scars left over from battles in Africa, and I asked him how he felt about the situation in the country. [ From the September 1964 issue: An eyewitness account of Cuba’s fumbling Marxism ] He answered with an expletive. I asked him what should be done to make things better. Cuba needed to be bombed, he told me. Specifically, Raúl Castro, Fidel’s brother and successor, should be bombed. And Raúl’s daughter Mariela. And the prime minister, Manuel Marrero Cruz. Again and again during my travels on the island, people told me: Cuba is not like this . They didn’t just mean the hunger and sickness and lack of electricity. They meant the anger, the emptiness, the absence of music and laughter. There used to be a musical group on every corner of Santiago, an 81-year-old man who had spent 45 years as a singer in a band recalled. Now there were none. After the 1959 revolution, Fidel Castro enshrined atheism in the new state, exiling many prominent Catholic figures and sending believers to reeducation camps. But in a sense, he did not so much banish religion as create a new cult, with its own rituals and holy martyrs. That cult staggers on today in a weird half life, abandoned by most of its people after decades of misery and repression, yet somehow defying a final collapse. Moises Saman / Magnum for The Atlantic Soldiers perform a changing-of-the-guard ceremony at Santa Ifigenia Cemetery in Santiago, where Fidel Castro’s remains are entombed. The only immaculately clean place I saw in all of Cuba was the Santa Ifigenia Cemetery, where Fidel’s ashes are held, in Santiago. The grass there is green and mowed to razor-perfection, the walkways carefully swept; not a single visitor was in sight when I went there. As I stood looking at the rounded granite boulder that marks Fidel’s tomb, patriotic music began blaring from invisible loudspeakers, and an honor guard of soldiers in neatly pressed uniforms began goose-stepping in unison, rifles pointed skyward. They marched to the mausoleum honoring José Martí, Cuba’s great nationalist hero; presented arms; and relieved a group of similarly uniformed compatriots, who marched back. They do this changing of the guard every half hour, all day long, I was told. Watching those perfect soldiers, you could believe for a moment that you were in another place—perhaps that far-off country Castro had dreamed of, where socialism is triumphant, no one is sick or unhappy, and everyone aspires to follow the heroic example of the man who led a glorious revolution. Then a breeze swept across the grass, carrying the acrid stench of burning garbage, and I remembered where I was. This article appears in the December 2026 print edition with the headline “How Castro’s Cuba Ends.”

items.title: Moustapha Guirassy : « Il ne faut pas coincer le Sénégal dans une logique trop technocratique, c’est un danger »
items.description: Prenant part, ce dimanche 25 octobre 2026, à la conférence de presse du gouvernement, le ministre de l’Éducation nationale, Moustapha Guirassy, a appelé les députés de Pastef-Les Patriotes à faire preuve de responsabilité, avant de les inviter à voter, mardi prochain, le projet de loi de finances rectificative (Lfr) 2026. « Enfermer la volonté des Sénégalais dans la coquille simplement d’un parti, ce serait rompre, en fait, avec les Sénégalais. Il ne faut pas coincer le Sénégal dans une logique trop technocratique, c’est un danger. Ce moment appelle un effort de tous pour comprendre ce qui se passe. Il y a la puissance, mais il y a une miséricorde et la capacité de pardonner. J’en appelle à la spiritualité parce que ce qui est en train de se jouer est critique », a déclaré le ministre. Par ailleurs, Moustapha Guirassy a rappelé l’effort consenti dans le recrutement de 8.000 enseignants entre 2024 et 2026. Selon lui, malgré des conditions très difficiles, l’effort dans le secteur social de l’éducation nationale se poursuit, notamment à travers les recrutements et la formation. « Alors qu’en 2023, il n’y avait que 800 personnes formées, ce chiffre a été multiplié par 113 dans les structures de formation, ce qui est du jamais vu. Malgré la situation difficile, 2.500 salles de classe ont été réalisées à l’élémentaire, démontrant que l’engagement de l’État est bien là », a-t-il fait savoir. Le ministre a également indiqué qu’un projet de création d’un Fonds autonome pour le financement de l’éducation était sur la table du président de la République. Une initiative qui, selon lui, va complètement changer la donne. « L’Éducation nationale est dans un processus de refondation avec des investissements massifs. Bien que les demandes soient pressantes, un sursaut est nécessaire pour franchir ce cap », a-t-il conclu. A. DIOUF

items.title: Diré : les leaders religieux mobilisés contre la poliomyélite
items.description: a Dire, les leaders religieux s'engagent a sensibiliser les parents a la lutte contre la poliomyelite. Cette mobilisation fait suite a la confirmation d'un cas dans la commune de Dangha, lors du premier tour de vaccination. La rencontre s'est tenue le dimanche 25 octobre 2026 en presence des partenaires de l'UNICEF et du service du Developpement social. L'objectif est de renforcer l'adhesion des communautes a la vaccination des enfants et de prevenir la propagation de la maladie. L’article Diré : les leaders religieux mobilisés contre la poliomyélite est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: Imaan, Hadi move SC against IHC order refusing to stay trial in security breach case
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Incarcerated human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, on Monday approached the Supreme Court to challenge the Islamabad High Court’s (IHC) Oct 19 order refusing to stay the trial before an anti-terrorism court (ATC) in the security breach case. The case pertains to the alleged disruption of the security route of an international cricket team and incitement to public unrest. The couple, accused of removing barriers from the route, was indicted on October 7. On Oct 19, the IHC took up appeals filed by Imaan and Hadi against the Oct 10 ATC order that rejected their petitions challenging the framing of charges and the inclusion of terrorism-related provisions. While issuing notices, the IHC had said it would decide how to proceed once the parties’ responses were received. Subsequently, the couple, through senior counsel Faisal Siddiqui, filed separate near-identical petitions before the SC on Monday, challenging the IHC’s Oct 19 order. The plea argued that the trial court proceeded with unprecedented haste by recording the examination-in-chief of six prosecution witnesses on Oct 10 and 14, and accepting the prosecution’s request to shift the trial to jail. The decision to conduct the trial in jail had also been challenged before the IHC, with the petition pointing out that the trial court had appointed state counsel . The petitions alleged that the ongoing trial was nothing but persecution aimed at subverting the SC’s order suspending the petitioners’ 17-year sentences in the controversial social media post case and at preventing their eventual release through an allegedly frivolous and mala fide case that had mysteriously resurfaced. Imaan’s petition argued that the IHC had “erroneously refused to exercise its discretion to grant ad interim relief to stay the criminal trial, despite multiple factual and legal reasons warranting such relief and repeated requests”. It said it was settled law that ad interim relief could not be denied in the presence of a prima facie case and where the balance of convenience favoured the petitioner, as she would otherwise suffer irreparable loss. The petition pleaded that Imaan had a clear prima facie case because recording evidence in their absence violated Section 353 (evidence to be taken in presence of accused) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), as well as their due process and fair trial rights guaranteed under the law. It further argued that the balance of convenience favoured the petitioner because delaying the trial for some time would not prejudice the prosecution. The plea claimed that the petitioner would suffer irreparable loss given the alleged gross violations of due process and fair trial principles in the proceedings, adding that it was apparent that the trial was leading to her criminal conviction. The petitioner’s liberty was at stake because of the denial of ad interim relief, the petition contended, adding that the IHC’s order was without jurisdiction, illegal and liable to be set aside. It further pointed out that the trial court had never dispensed with the petitioner’s personal attendance during the recording of evidence and that no proceedings under Section 540-A (power to summon material witness or examine person present) of the CrPC had been initiated. The trial court’s order of Oct 10 recorded that counsel had left the rostrum and the accused had left the video link. The Oct 14 order also noted that the accused had again moved away from the camera while their counsel had left the rostrum during the examination-in-chief of witnesses. Despite this, the court proceeded to record the examination-in-chief of six prosecution witnesses on the two dates. The petitions emphasised that the absence of the petitioners and their counsel was forced as a protest and had been recorded as such, but did not amount to a waiver of the right to be present during the recording of evidence. IHC hears plea against jail trial, appointment of state counsel Meanwhile, the IHC heard arguments on a petition filed by Imaan and Hadi challenging their trial at Adiala jail and the appointment of a state counsel . A division bench comprising Justice Raja Inaam Ameen Minhas and Justice Shahrukh Arjumand continued the proceedings, with advocates Riasat Ali Azad and Zainab Janjua appearing for the petitioners. During the proceedings, Advocate Azad noted that the decision to conduct the trial inside the jail had been challenged before the IHC. He contended that the accused should have been heard before such an arrangement was approved. Justice Minhas questioned the legal basis of the challenge, asking who had the authority to decide the venue of a trial and whether an accused could dictate where the proceedings should take place. In response, Azad said the petitioners were being brought before what he described as a “jail court”, effectively a cage, where access to the proceedings was restricted. He argued that the summary for conducting the jail trial had been initiated by an Islamabad superintendent of police and subsequently approved by the chief commissioner. According to him, the police officer lacked the authority to initiate such a summary, which he maintained fell within the federal government’s domain. The judge questioned whether a summary concerning a jail trial would have to be placed before the cabinet and also asked about the legal concept of an open court. Azad said he had not been heard before the decision was taken, despite the need to hear the defence. He pointed out that journalists and members of the public were not permitted to attend the proceedings inside the jail. He further submitted that the defence had requested the trial judge to pass a formal judicial order regarding the arrangement, but the judge declined, telling the lawyers to challenge the matter before the high court. The lawyer also objected to the appointment of a state counsel during the jail trial. Justice Minhas observed that the defence lawyers’ vakalatnamas (powers of attorney authorising legal representation) were still on the court record. Advocate Janjua clarified that she had initially represented the accused but subsequently withdrew her vakalatnama , explaining that travelling to Adiala jail every day was incompatible with managing her legal practice. Azad added that travelling to and from the jail took around two hours each way. When the judge again asked whether his vakalatnama remained on record, Azad said the defence had effectively been sidelined. He alleged that when he sought a single adjournment, a state counsel was appointed and the cross-examination of prosecution witnesses was conducted in his absence. Questioning the urgency of the proceedings, Azad said the first information report (FIR) had remained concealed for two years and that the accused had been arrested in the case immediately after securing bail from the SC. He further contended that although the original charges were bailable, a terrorism-related charge had subsequently been added. The counsel requested the IHC to restrain the trial court from delivering its final verdict until the petition was decided. Justice Minhas observed that the accused could also be acquitted, asking the lawyer why he was seeking such an order. Advocate Azad reiterated the request that the trial court be restrained from announcing its final verdict. After hearing the arguments, Justice Minhas remarked that the court would examine the matter. The bench did not announce a final decision on the request during the proceedings.

items.title: Entre deux élections
items.description: Conquérir le pouvoir, distribuer les places, compter les fidèles : mais que reste-t-il au citoyen une fois les urnes rangées ? Derrière les querelles de direction, les congrès et la mise en conformité des partis politiques gabonais, une exigence peine à s’imposer : celle de leur utilité pour le peuple. Ike Ngouoni Aila Oyouomi* interroge cet écart entre les ambitions des appareils politiques et les attentes de ceux qui votent. Avec une question qui engage toutes les formations : que permettent-elles de changer à ceux qui ne réclament aucun poste ? À quoi sert un parti politique s’il ne porte pas les attentes du peuple jusqu’à la rive où l’on décide ? (illustration IA) © GabonReview/Midjourney Avant l'échéance de mise en conformité, le Gabon comptait cent quatre partis politiques. Ces dernières semaines, trois affaires les ont remis en pleine lumière : la réforme de la loi qui les encadre, contestée devant la Cour constitutionnelle, la querelle de l'ancien parti dominant sur la question de savoir qui le dirige légitimement, et le congrès du parti au pouvoir, fixé au 5 décembre. Une loi, une querelle, un congrès. Dans aucune des trois, la question centrale n'est ce que ces partis font pour ceux qui votent. Cela dit moins l'état d'esprit de leurs dirigeants que la fonction que ces organisations remplissent. Un parti, chez nous, sert d'abord deux publics. Ceux qui visent le pouvoir y trouvent une porte, un rang, une proximité. Ceux qui l'exercent y trouvent une légitimité, un réservoir de noms et une majorité à portée de vote. Ces deux utilités sont réelles et ne scandalisent personne. Elles ne sont simplement pas celles que le citoyen attend. Cette fonction n'a rien de neuf. Le Parti démocratique gabonais est né en 1968 comme parti unique, et pendant plus de vingt ans appartenir au parti fut le chemin le plus court vers un poste. La Conférence nationale de 1990 a rouvert le pluralisme. L'habitude de voir dans le parti une porte d'entrée plutôt qu'un service a survécu aux changements de sigle et de régime. Les partis ne sont pas absents entre deux scrutins. Certains réunissent des habitants, installent des coordinations de quartier, recueillent des doléances. Les Gabonais, eux non plus, ne se désintéressent pas de la politique : ils en suivent les nominations, les disgrâces, les rapprochements. Cette activité est réelle. La question est de savoir ce qu'elle produit. Une rencontre peut servir à écouter, à recruter, à entretenir une fidélité, à préparer une candidature, et ces fonctions coexistent. Ce que le citoyen attend de plus tient en peu de chose : qu'on lui explique une décision, qu'on rassemble les difficultés que chacun affronte isolément, qu'on les porte devant les responsables et qu'on revienne lui dire ce qui a été obtenu. On dit chez nous qu'on ne traverse pas le fleuve sans connaître ses courants. Un parti devrait être ce passeur, celui qui connaît à la fois la rive où l'on vit et la rive où l'on décide, et qui sait ce que chacune attend de l'autre. Plus d'une centaine de pirogues ont été mises à l'eau. Toutes ne font pas la traversée : ce que les gens disent devient trop rarement ce que décide une institution. Il y a aussi cette crainte de rester l'« Okoukoute », celui qui regarde passer les occasions pendant que d'autres trouvent leur place. Elle nourrit un rapport ambivalent au pouvoir : on en dénonce les avantages tout en redoutant d'en être durablement exclu. Le parti devient alors un lieu où chacun espère trouver une issue personnelle, bien avant d'y construire une réponse commune. Je pense à un jeune de vingt ou trente ans. Sa question est autre : « Qu'est-ce que je peux y faire ? » Peut-il y défendre une idée, contester une orientation, conduire une initiative et voir son travail compter ? On ne peut pas lui demander de s'engager si tout est décidé avant son arrivée. Une place dans un cortège ou dans un bureau de jeunesse ne lui donne pas nécessairement une voix. Encore faut-il que son engagement puisse changer quelque chose dans le parti, puis à travers lui. La querelle de l'ancien parti dominant pose une question de droit interne légitime : à qui appartient un sigle quand ses dirigeants se contestent. Elle se règle entre membres, devant les instances ou devant les juges, sans que l'électeur y ait voix. Le premier congrès ordinaire du parti au pouvoir dira beaucoup de l'organisation d'une formation jeune. Reste à savoir quelle place il donnera aux engagements envers ceux qui l'ont portée. La réforme de la loi compte, trie, met en conformité, et il y a de bonnes raisons de faire le ménage parmi plus d'une centaine de formations. Cette arithmétique ne dit pas l'essentiel : combien de ces partis, une fois déclarés en règle, auront quelque chose à offrir à un citoyen un mardi ordinaire ? Un parti peut survivre à la loi, à la querelle et au congrès sans avoir servi à grand monde en dehors de ses membres. Les partis ont des statuts pour dire qui les dirige, des lois pour dire s'ils sont en règle, des congrès pour se compter. Il faudra savoir devant qui ils rendent compte, entre deux scrutins, de ce qu'ils font pour le citoyen. Cette exigence vaut aussi pour ceux qui ont créé un parti. Entre deux élections, que permettent les partis à ceux qui ne cherchent ni investiture ni nomination, mais veulent peser sur la vie du pays ? Ike NGOUONI AILA OYOUOMI * Président, AILA, Cabinet de conseil stratégique L’article Entre deux élections est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Tagadayat : l’armée annonce la découverte de 54 corps
items.description: © Internet Une patrouille a retrouvé 54 corps dans un campement situé au sud-est de Ménaka, selon l’état-major général des Armées. Neuf rescapés ont été évacués vers la ville pour recevoir des soins. L’état-major général des Armées a annoncé samedi 24 octobre la découverte de 54 corps dans un campement de Tagadayat, à environ 35 kilomètres au sud-est de Ménaka. La patrouille avait été envoyée dans la zone après des informations faisant état d’attaques contre des populations civiles. Les victimes ont été inhumées sur place. Neuf personnes retrouvées vivantes ont été transportées à Ménaka et confiées aux services chargés de leur prise en charge. L’armée affirme que les premiers témoignages recueillis attribuent les tueries à l’État islamique au Grand Sahara. Cette attribution constitue la version officielle communiquée par l’état-major. Les comptes rendus consultés ne font état d’aucune revendication authentifiée du groupe. Un bilan actualisé après les premières alertes L’attaque avait été signalée le dimanche 18 octobre. Le lendemain, le bureau exécutif de la communauté Idaksahak avait annoncé la mort d’au moins 48 civils à Tagadayat. Il faisait également état de blessés et de déplacements de familles vers Ménaka. Le chiffre de 54 annoncé par l’armée correspond aux corps découverts pendant les recherches sur le terrain. Il actualise le premier bilan communautaire de 48 victimes. Les deux nombres concernent la même attaque et ne doivent pas être additionnés. Les informations publiées permettent désormais de retenir plusieurs éléments précis. L’attaque remonte au 18 octobre, la découverte annoncée porte sur 54 corps, neuf rescapés ont été évacués et les recherches se sont déroulées dans un campement situé à 35 kilomètres de Ménaka. L’identité complète des victimes et la répartition entre hommes, femmes et enfants restent absentes des comptes rendus publics. Le nombre de familles ayant quitté les campements voisins n’a pas davantage été chiffré. Des habitants déplacés vers Ménaka L’état-major indique avoir renforcé les mesures de protection et facilité le déplacement vers Ménaka des habitants de campements exposés. Des patrouilles et des opérations de sécurisation se poursuivent dans le secteur. La communauté Idaksahak avait demandé une assistance urgente pour les personnes déplacées. Les besoins cités concernent l’accueil, l’alimentation, les soins et la protection des civils. Leur évaluation locale repose maintenant sur le recensement des familles arrivées à Ménaka et sur la situation des campements encore occupés. L’annonce du 24 octobre apporte ainsi un bilan officiel issu des recherches menées à Tagadayat. Elle confirme l’ampleur des pertes civiles signalées six jours auparavant et fait état de mouvements de populations vers Ménaka. Les prochains bilans des services locaux devront préciser le nombre de déplacés et l’assistance effectivement déployée.

items.title: Comment l’Amérique latine réagit à la victoire de Lula
items.description: Le président brésilien Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a été réélu hier, dimanche 25 octobre, pour un quatrième mandat contre Flávio Bolsonaro, le fils de l’ex-président Jair Bolsonaro, assigné à résidence après avoir été condamné à 27 ans de prison pour tentative de coup d’État. La cérémonie d’investiture aura lieu le 5 janvier 2027. À cette heure, les gouvernements de la moitié des pays de la région (16 sur 32) ont adressé leurs félicitations à Lula, et aucune réaction officielle n’a été relevée pour 13 d’entre eux. Le Costa Rica est le seul pays d’Amérique latine dont le gouvernement a « félicité le peuple brésilien d’avoir […] élu son nouveau président dans un processus démocratique et pacifique », sans toutefois nommer Lula. En Colombie, le président Abelardo de la Espriella, qui avait soutenu Flávio Bolsonaro, a reconnu la victoire de Lula sans le féliciter : « Ni Lula ne décide pour les Colombiens, ni moi pour les Brésiliens », et a évoqué de « grandes et profondes différences politiques et idéologiques » avec le président brésilien. En la campaña presidencial colombiana, el presidente Lula apoyó abiertamente a Iván Cepeda y gané yo. En la campaña brasileña, apoyé a Bolsonaro y ganó Lula. Ni Lula decide por los colombianos ni yo decido por los brasileños. ¡DECIDE LA GENTE ! Y cuando el pueblo se pronuncia en… — Abelardo De La Espriella (@ABDELAESPRIELLA) October 26, 2026 En Argentine, le gouvernement de Javier Milei n’a pas encore publié de communiqué au sujet de l’élection brésilienne, et le président n’a pas félicité Lula. En amont du scrutin, Milei avait écrit sur le réseau social X espérer que le « dernier tour de campagne sale » de Lula « n’inclue pas de voler l’élection ». Le jour du vote, il a partagé des publications accusant Lula de vouloir « voler » l’élection. – Paraliza el conteo de votos – Mete preso al Sec. de Transporte de Bahía por no permitir su fraude y acarreo – Pide al Juez Supremo (que es su amigo) que extienda el tiempo de votación – Ya sabe los resultados de la elección, pero no los publica, mientras se sigue votando pic.twitter.com/txYTBcbwC4 — El Trumpista (@ElTrumpista) October 25, 2026 Dans ses stories Instagram, Milei a partagé une image avec la légende « Lula voleur et menteur », selon le quotidien argentin Perfil . Il a également publié une image générée par l’IA le représentant aux côtés de Flávio Bolsonaro, avec une citation attribuée à ce dernier : « J’ai confiance dans le fait que le Brésil pourra se relever » Del “Lula ladrón” al mutismo : el Gobierno nacional no habla de la victoria del PT en Brasil », Perfil , 25 octobre 2026.'> 4 . La victoire de Lula, avec plus de 4 millions de voix d’avance sur Flávio Bolsonaro, interrompt la série de victoires enregistrées par des candidats proches ou alignés sur Donald Trump, depuis 2025. Mis à part au Suriname, où la candidate de gauche Jennifer Geerlings-Simons avait été élue en juillet 2025, tous les scrutins majeurs avaient débouché sur l’élection d’un dirigeant proche de Washington. La réélection de Trump, en novembre 2024, avait coïncidé avec un effet domino qu’il semble avoir au moins en partie entraîné : en plus du Pérou, l’Équateur, la Bolivie, le Chili, le Costa Rica, la Colombie et le Honduras avaient élu des présidents de droite et d’extrême droite. Sur les cinq principales économies de la région, le Brésil et le Mexique, qui représentent plus de la moitié du PIB de l’Amérique latine, sont les seuls pays dirigés par un président de gauche. L’article Comment l’Amérique latine réagit à la victoire de Lula est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Affaire Kamel Daoud : sa femme sort du silence
items.description: Mise en cause dans l’affaire du roman “Houris”, la femme de Kamel Daoud sort du silence. Aicha Dahdouh s’est exprimée dans un communiqué transmis dimanche 25 octobre à l’AFP, alors que le tribunal d’Oran devrait rendre son verdict ce mardi. Tout en clamant son innocence, la femme se démarque des positions de l’écrivain sur l'Algérie, l'islam et la Palestine. Aïcha Dahdouh, psychiatre, est soupçonnée d'avoir divulgué un secret médical en racontant l’histoire d’une de ses patientes à son mari qui l’a mise en roman. Le roman en question, “Houris”, a remporté le prix Goncourt 2024. Aicha Dahdouh, femme de Kamel Daoud : “Je suis innocente” Saada Arbane, une rescapée d’un attentat terroriste en Algérie dans les années 1990, a reconnu sa propre histoire à travers le personnage principal de l’œuvre et a saisi la justice. Mme Arbane a soutenu que la seule personne qui pouvait divulguer à Kamel Daoud les détails de son drame c'est sa femme Aicha Dahdouh, qui n’est autre que la psychiatre qui la suivait. “Je suis innocente. Je n'ai pas divulgué de secret médical. Je n'ai pas volé de dossier », a indiqué la femme de l’écrivain dans son communiqué transmis à l’AFP. “Le secret médical est l'un des fondements de l'éthique médicale, et je lui ai toujours été fidèle », s’est-elle défendue. “Je ne partage pas ses positions sur l'Algérie, l'islam et la Palestine” S’agissant du procès de son mari en Algérie, dans lequel elle est également poursuivie, Aicha Dahdouh a indiqué qu'elle aurait souhaité s’y présenter mais, explique-t-elle, elle a été empêchée par « le retentissement des positions de Kamel Daoud et une situation familiale douloureuse ». La femme de Kamel Daoud s’est exprimée à la même occasion sur les positions controversées de l’écrivain, qu'elle dit clairement ne pas partager. « La voix de Kamel Daoud ne doit pas effacer la mienne », écrit-elle, assurant qu'elle « ne partage pas » ses positions sur « trois questions essentielles, l'Algérie, l'islam et la Palestine ». « Plus profondément encore, ce qui nous sépare, c'est le regard porté sur la douleur d'autrui », a écrit Aicha Dahdouh à propos de son époux. Kamel Daoud a toujours soutenu que sa femme est hors de cause dans cette affaire. L’article Affaire Kamel Daoud : sa femme sort du silence est apparu en premier sur TSA .
